title: How to improve customer experience beyond dashboards
summary: Learn how B2B teams can improve customer experience by strengthening operational visibility, workflow coordination, and customer support consistency.
body_markdown:
Learn how B2B teams can improve customer experience by strengthening operational visibility, workflow coordination, and customer support consistency.


According to Front’s[Coordination Tax Report](https://front.com/resources/coordination-tax-report) , only 5% of companies have complete visibility into handoffs, coordination time, and duplicate work. And 95% of them try to fix the customer experience (CX) with faster replies and more channels.


That’s treating the symptom while the real failure happens in the coordination gaps behind the scenes. When teams don’t share feedback and customer context, they’re not working from the same picture, and the customer feels the gap before anyone on your team does.


Here’s what’s driving the problem, how to improve CX where it counts, and what CX implementation looks like once you’re past the dashboards.


## What positive CX means in B2B operations


CX is the full experience a customer has with your company, from first contact through the last renewal conversation, not just the interactions they can see.


B2B CX operates at a different scale than B2C, with higher stakes attached to every miscommunication. Support here isn’t just conversations; it’s onboarding, renewals, and all the inter-team scheduling and cross-functional work a customer never sees but always feels the effects of. Every internal handoff shapes what the customer experience is next, which is why fixing CX means looking at the whole operation and not just the visible touch points.


## The operational issues behind inconsistent CX


Inconsistent CX is a symptom, not a root cause. Here’s what’s usually driving it.


### Context that never leaves the thread it started in


When an important detail lives in a private conversation between two reps instead of a shared workspace, the next person to pick up the case doesn’t have it. They either stall and circle back, or ask the customer to repeat themselves. The team loses time and the customer loses confidence.


### Lack of ownership and visibility


“Did someone reach out to this customer?” “I thought you were driving the onboarding timeline.” Threads like these happen when no one owns the handoff. B2B relationships run on long-term retention and a customer-focused experience, and retention doesn’t survive a blame game. When scope isn’t clear, customers wait for someone who can help, and often, nobody realizes they’re still waiting.


### Slow handoffs that compound over time


Front’s Coordination Tax report found that B2B companies spend[nearly three hours coordinating](https://research.front.com/) for every hour spent solving customer problems.


When customer history lives across disconnected tools and spreadsheets, every handoff starts from a partial picture, and missed onboarding milestones or billing issues can go unnoticed until they’ve already cost you the relationship.


### Customers re-proving what they’ve already told you


[64% of companies](https://research.front.com/) experienced at least one customer-facing coordination failure in the last three months. Most trace back to the same root cause: one platform holds the current issue, another holds the history, and neither rep can see the full picture. The customer ends up verifying their identity and re-explaining their problem (sometimes more than once, across different channels) for something they already resolved.


## How to fix CX at the root, not the surface


To improve your CX strategy, you need more than metrics. Operational consistency across teams and customer conversations can help. Here are some CX best practices.


### 1. Centralize customer conversations and context


When all communication ties back to one shared space, everyone has what they need without asking around. A billing issue that touches both finance and[customer support](https://front.com/blog/omnichannel-customer-support) , for example, doesn’t need three separate email threads. It needs one collaboration thread tied to the customer’s full context, so the right people can resolve it without losing accuracy along the way.


### 2. Standardize response consistency across workflows


Arbitrary response times and unclear SLAs make it impossible to do a CX evaluation honestly. Fix this with single-owner accountability — a named person or team owns the interaction and hands it off with full context intact. Tiering also helps: a two-hour window for high-value accounts, longer for others, reduces delays and keeps SLAs from quietly slipping.


### 3. Strengthen cross-functional collaboration


Every team touching a customer issue is contributing to the same CX outcome. Bring teams into marketing and sales planning early so they can adjust roadmaps proactively and give everyone visibility into the same workspace for[cross-functional collaboration](https://front.com/blog/cross-functional-collaboration-for-better-customer-experiences) , including mentions, comments, and shared context. This way, operational silos stop hiding workload from the people who need to see it.


### 4. Pair automation with human oversight


Automation and[AI-assisted workflows](https://front.com/blog/state-of-service-expectations-ai-comfort-gap) speed up responses and absorb repetitive queries, but they can’t fully replace judgment. Rule-based automation is consistent by design — the same question gets the same answer, every time, regardless of who’s on shift — but complex or edge-case interactions need a human reading the room. Over-automate, and you lose the nuance that catches the exception the standard answer doesn’t fit.


### 5. Measure CX operationally, not just anecdotally


Front’s same report found that[over a third of companies](https://research.front.com/) lost a top performer due to coordination burnout in the past year. This shows that coordination is a delicate balance, and you need the right operational systems in place to make sure it isn’t making more work for every team member.


Customers feel the same breakdown from the outside: long waits, inaccurate resolutions, escalations caused by reps who never had the context to begin with. Before making changes, find the gaps. Has CSAT dipped? What’s the trend on retention? Where have response and resolution times started slipping? Build your fixes from there.


## CX runs on coordination, Front is where B2B teams keep it


Improving the customer journey is hard enough without[disconnected conversations](https://front.com/blog/how-to-connect-with-customers) , workflows, and internal coordination working against you.


Front keeps every conversation, handoff, and piece of context connected, so customer experience stays consistent even as volume grows. Collaboration tools keep handoffs intact without losing detail, automation takes on repetitive work under human supervision, and every part of your operation moves together instead of against each other.


The results teams see include SLAs that are easier to hit, faster resolutions, and customers who experience your teams as one, not several.
